title: Criteria to evaluate neurogenic bladder in patients  with Congenital Zika Syndrome
author: Lucia Maria Costa Monteiro

steps_raw.instruction: Criteria to evaluate neurogenic bladder in children with Congenital Zika Syndrome
Authors: Lucia M. Costa Monteiro, Glaura N. O. Cruz, Juliana M. Fontes e Marcia C.B. Boechat
Institution: Instituto Nacional de Saúde da Mulher, Criança e Adolescente Fernandes Figueira (IFF/FIOCRUZ), Rio de Janeiro, Brasil.
Protocol Recommendation: referrer all children with confirmed Congenital Zika Syndrome for urological assessment, as followed:
Initial assessment of urological screening:

The initial assessment, in agreement with our experience (1) and the International Children’s Continence Society (2), comprised a detailed clinical history, a comprehensive physical examination and urinalysis and culture to determine if the child will need to be further evaluated.
Clinical history including:
prenatal and maternal history (rash during pregnancy and/or low fever, myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, conjunctival hyperemia), gestational period of exposure to Zika, perinatal complications

Investigation of bladder habits in infants including the number of diapers used per day, the wetness of diapers and the interval between changes (continence interval). It is important to investigate symptoms of urinary tract infection (UTI), including changes in the color and aspect of urine, fever and dysuria.

Investigation of bowel habits including water ingestion and type of diet, any special regimen for bowel emptying, the frequency of bowel emptying and the characteristic of stool - we recommend the use of the Bristol Stool Scale) (3).
Physical examination: including (apart from the overall systemic evaluation):
Evaluation of blood pressure
Inspection of abdomen: bladder and bowel
Evaluation of Central nervous system: head circumference (to confirm microcephaly), spine and upper and lower extremities irregularities, perineal sensation and reflexes.
urinalysis and culture for all patients during the initial assessment
urinalysis and culture in all febrile episodes to exclude UTI
Note: we recommend urethral catheterization for urinalysis and culture.
Second phase of the urological screening:
Further investigation of the urological system:
Lab tests: complete blood count (CBC), blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine (if these were not already performed at the CZS screening)
Urinary ultrasonography based on kidney, ureter and bladder evaluation(4)

Kidney: to investigate length, outline (smooth, irregular or global thinning), cortico-medullar differentiation, calyceal/pelvic dilatation. The pelvic diameter measured transversely may be considered normal if ≤ 7 mm in neonates and
≤ 10 mm in older children. Report any degree of renal dilatation found in patients with Congenital Zika Syndrome.
Ureters: to investigate the presence of ureteral dilatation (longitudinal and transverse diameter).
Bladder: pre-voiding evaluation (bladder wall, contents, and volume) and post-void residual (PVR) whenever possible (conditional to children age and cooperation).
Urodynamic study (UDS):

UDS tests: For neurogenic bladder, urodynamic diagnosis are based on bladder and urethral sphincter behavior during filling and voiding phases. Early diagnosis improves prognostic(1) (Costa Monteiro, 2016).
CMG: performed after ruling out UTI, to determine bladder capacity, contractility, compliance, emptying ability and degree of continence.
Urethral catheterization is performed under topic anesthesia with lidocaine gel (1%), using ideally a double lumen pediatric catheter.
Bladder pressure is measured before emptying the bladder
The initial urinary residual volume is measured, considering diaper wetness and/or voiding before or during catheterization.
Filling rate is calculated based on 5 to 10% of the expected bladder capacity for age (ml/min).
Maximum bladder capacity is measured just before child voids, baseline bladder pressure stays above 40 cm of H2O or the volume infused is 1,5 times the expected capacity for the age.
Maximum bladder pressure is measured at the bladder capacity,
Leak point pressure is measured at first leak
Voiding pressure is measured when void starts.
Post void residual (PVR) measured at the end of the exam
Note: Whenever possible, pressure measurements are made considering the baseline, outside a bladder contraction.
Bladder behavior is classified into one of four categories:
normal bladder (relaxed during filling, sustained bladder contraction upon reaching maximum capacity with relaxed sphincter, complete emptying without post-void residue);
underactive bladder (relaxed during filling and incapable of generating or sustaining contraction that allow complete bladder emptying);
overactive bladder (detrusor contractions during filling, elevated intravesical pressures, and early emptying before reaching maximum bladder capacity)
low bladder compliance (loss of bladder capacity to remain relaxed during filling, progressive increase in intravesical pressure, elevated bladder pressures, and early emptying)
EMG: to measure sphincter activity during filling and voiding phase
EMG was performed using patch EMG electrodes

Sphincter is normal (detrusor sphincter synergia) when sphincter activity remains present during the filling phase and reduces following a high bladder pressure during contraction, a leak or a voiding.
Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia (DSD) occurs when the sphincter failed to relax, or increases activity during high bladder pressure contraction, leak or voiding.

Pediatric urodynamics is challenging and requires trained professionals. Parents and the child need to be previously familiarized with urodynamic procedures and catheterization. Room are adapted to promote a child friendly environment with toys and video/television showing children's films. Both parents are encouraged to stay in the room during the entire procedure so as to comfort and support the child.
Third phase of the urological screening:
Chloridrate of oxibutine/anticholinergic drugs: to control overactive bladder and low bladder compliance.

Intermittent clean catheterization (CIC): whenever bladder emptying is ineffective, with recurrent urinary tract infections, renal and ureteral dilatation or presence of grade 4 and 5 Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) (5)

Antibiotics: for treatment of urinary tract infections confirmed clinically and through laboratory exams, according to the susceptibility test, as well as a prophylactic measure, according to the clinical and laboratory history of recurrent urinary tract infections.
Note: To increase treatment adherence, parents are trained to perform CIC. A specialized nurse is responsible for training and follow-up.
Voiding cystourethography (VCUG): to determine the presence or absence of bladder and urethral abnormalities, including vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).
ureteral or pelvic dilatation at renal US
high bladder pressure.
Renal scan (DMSA and DTPA):
DMSA: to evaluate renal morphology, particularly for detection of scarring and pyelonephritis
follow-up of pyelonephritis.
DTPA: to evaluate kidney excretion
High detrusor filling pressure
Urethral sphincter dyssynergia
Clinical re-evaluation every three to six months, depending on risk factors and treatment response.
Parents oriented to seek advise if any change in the color and/or smell of the patient’s urine is observed or if patient presents fever episodes without a known cause.
UDS and renal and bladder US repeated at an interval of six months to one year, depending on the risk factors presented.
